reject_reason: generic musings on unnamed ruined forts and gadhis across India; no specific Udaypur evidence

items.note: Local-area lore about treasure seekers who dig at the gadhi with picks and spades; author concedes someone may find something.
items.gloss: Greedy people still come to the gadhi. They do not come in a crowd to fight anyone with guns and swords. They come quietly with pickaxes and spades. To test their luck they dig up rubble anywhere and go away. It is possible someone does find something.

reject_reason: generic appeal to youth and teachers plus unsupported speculation about the gadhi; nothing quotable as evidence

items.note: Author's proposal to the government: compulsory heritage walks in schools and colleges, easy tourist circuits with two or three monuments in a day, mission-mode work from minister to village panch.
items.gloss: We have also suggested to the government that heritage walks should be made compulsory in schools and colleges at state and district level. College and university students should go and see the great heritage present across the country. Senior school students should be taken to such places in their own state, and younger students should be taken to district or block level heritage at least twice a year. For this the tourism department can develop easy tourist circuits with routes covering two or three monuments in one day. From government to panchayat, from a minister to a village panch, everyone can contribute actively. This is mission-mode work, not for filling files with papers and orders.

items.note: Proposals to connect new generations with heritage: good publications on local history and archaeology kept in schools and colleges, short films, and heritage as a central theme in writing and speech contests.
items.gloss: For this, high-quality short and detailed publications on local history and archaeology should be made and kept in schools and colleges themselves. Short films should be made and broadcast in the digital world. Our heritage should be made a compulsory central theme in writing and speech competitions among children. Through this they will be eager to read about their history and go and see it.

reject_reason: generic reflections on studying history and on stones being silent; no specific Udaypur evidence

items.note: Shivkumar Vivek credits Udayaditya with creating Udaypur wholeheartedly, as a descendant of Bhoja and governor at the last edge of the kingdom; he built Udayasagar and the Nilakantheshwar temple, one of the most beautiful temples.
items.gloss: Udayaditya had created Udaypur with his full heart. This descendant of Raja Bhoja was the governor at this last edge of the state. He had Udayasagar built. He raised the Nilakantheshwar temple. One of the most beautiful temples of the country. A matchless specimen of architecture.

claim.value: Udayaditya created Udaypur; built Udayasagar and the temple (Vivek)

items.note: Describes many replicas of the temple stacked one over another from base to shikhara, with no place empty of sculpture and carving.
items.gloss: From the base to the shikhara several replicas of the temple itself are kept stacked one upon another. No place is empty of sculptures and carving.

items.note: Author states that at some time attackers came and struck hammers and chisels at the sculptures; compares them to those who destroyed the Bamiyan Buddhas (author's characterisation).
items.gloss: At some period some tyrants came here. They struck hammers on the matchless sculptures made by some artist devoted to art. They struck chisels at the worshipped images. They were not of another faith but people devoid of religious culture. People like these we have seen with our own eyes destroying the Buddhas of Bamiyan.

items.note: Notes damage to sculptures: broken hands, missing heads, clear marks of blows.
items.gloss: Look carefully at some images: someone's hand is broken, some heads are missing. On many the marks of blows are clear. They kept resisting the blows steadily. They could not be broken.

items.note: Author attributes the destruction to followers of Muhammad Tughlaq who wished to turn temples into mosques (author's attribution, not a cited source).
items.gloss: The weapons of hundreds of Muhammad Tughlaq's irritable, heartless, senseless followers must have become blunt. They were mad. They wanted to break temples and settle the house of God. They set out to break the place of worship of thousands and make their own place of prayer.

items.note: Says images were inscribed with Urdu messages and a mosque begun from temple remains, with half-built mosque walls visible from the temple precinct.
items.gloss: They wrote messages of God on them in Urdu. The work of building a mosque from the remains of the temple began. Look behind the mosque's stones and some image will be stuck there. A plan was made to cover the temple. Standing in the temple complex, the half-finished walls of the mosque give evidence of this.

items.note: States that a madrasa occupies Udayaditya's thousand-year-old palace, Udayasagar is farmed, and encroachment has gripped the Nilakantheshwar temple.
items.gloss: A madrasa came to occupy Udayaditya's thousand-year-old palace. Cultivation began on Udayasagar. Encroachment gripped the Nilakantheshwar temple.

items.note: Vijay Manohar Tiwari, journalist and state information commissioner from the district, took historian Dr. Suresh Mishra to Udaypur; a group of enthusiastic youths organised to make people aware of the heritage.
items.gloss: He resolved to bring it out of the dark lanes. He took the history expert Dr. Suresh Mishra and, weaving the threads of past events, searched the cruel cycle of time. A group of enthusiastic youths organised. Since then they have been busy making people aware of this heritage.

items.note: Shivkumar Vivek visited and found many people active for conservation; he laments gram panchayats' unconcern; grassroots work planned in memory of Dr. Suresh Mishra.
items.gloss: When I too reached here last Sunday with such curiosities, I found that many people had become active in the direction of conserving this heritage. The thorn that pricks is why gram panchayats and village clusters remain unconcerned about preserving the great heritage lying within them. Tiwari gives the happy news that, in memory of Dr. Suresh Mishra who passed away in the recent Corona period, a plan to do some grassroots work to preserve the heritage around them and awaken historical consciousness is being considered.

items.note: Ajit Vadnerkar's post: Udaypur (Vidisha) about to change; people interested in history, archaeology and heritage are visiting; local enthusiasm that long-neglected monuments will revive.
items.gloss: The days of Udaypur (Vidisha) are about to turn. People interested in the protection and promotion of history, archaeology and cultural treasures are coming here continuously. Among local people there is enthusiasm that Udaypur's monuments, victims of centuries of neglect, will now come alive.

items.note: Suggests that merchants of Vidisha, Ganj Basoda and Mandi Bamora could themselves become guardians of the monuments scattered between Malwa and Bundelkhand.
items.gloss: If the leading merchants of Vidisha, Ganj Basoda and Mandi Bamora wish, they themselves can come forward as protectors of these unattended scattered monuments between Malwa and Bundelkhand.

items.note: States that Malwa was known in the centuries BCE as Dasharna and Avanti, jointly under Ashoka, with Vidisha centre of eastern Malwa and Ujjayini of western Malwa.
items.gloss: Today's Malwa was known in the centuries BCE by two names, Dasharna and Avanti. This vast region was jointly under Ashoka. Later it came to be called Malwa. Vidisha was the centre of eastern Malwa and Ujjayini of western Malwa.

items.note: Lists Khilji, Tughlaq, Lodi and Mughal as invaders whose attacks the Malwa-Bundelkhand regions suffered.
items.gloss: Khilji... Tughlaq... Lodi and then Mughal... The glorious janapadas of Malwa-Bundelkhand bore the pain of the ill-intentioned attacks of all these.

items.note: Udaypur is about seventy km from Vidisha and today not even a qasba; a sleeping village that once was the temple-town of the ancient Dasharna kingdom.
items.gloss: About seventy km from Vidisha, Udaypur today cannot even be called a qasba. A sleeping village that waits to wake from its past... A thousand years ago when it went into slumber, its splendour must have been that of a temple-town of the ancient Dasharna kingdom.

items.note: History lies buried under almost all of Udaypur; ruins visible, many converted into pucca houses, and the old and new patches are visible to any ordinary tourist.
items.gloss: History lies buried in the foundations of almost the whole of Udaypur. Much can be seen in the ruins, but many ruins have been converted into pucca houses. No expert's eye is needed to identify these patches of ancient and modern. The eye of any ordinary tourist can also identify them.

items.note: Udayeshvara Mahadeva regarded as the finest Paramara-period construction, called Bhumija in architectural terminology, a style for building on sloping ground, with walls of brick and stone (as stated by this author).
items.gloss: Udayeshvara Mahadeva is considered the best specimen of Paramara-period construction. In the classical terminology of architecture it is called Bhumija architecture, which was a distinctive style of building on level and sloping ground. In it walls were made of brick and stone.

claim.value: Bhumija = style for level and sloping ground; brick and stone walls (Vadnerkar)

items.note: Scholars say the Bhumija style was born, developed and refined in Malwa, especially in the 9th-10th century Paramara period, and spread to Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh.
items.gloss: Scholars say that the Bhumija style of architecture was born, elevated and developed in Malwa, especially in the Paramara period of the ninth-tenth century. From here the style spread also to Rajasthan, Malwa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh.

claim.value: born and developed in Malwa, 9th-10th c. Paramara period (scholars, per Vadnerkar)

items.note: On a heritage walk early in the year, Suresh Mishra and Vijay Manohar Tiwari found a private-property notice on the old palace ruins and green cloths spread over stones among the ruins.
items.gloss: At the beginning of this year the famous historian Dr. Suresh Mishra and state information commissioner Vijay Manohar Tiwari were on a heritage walk in this city of history. What this pair saw there was astonishing. During this they found that a notice of private property was pasted on the ruins of the old royal palace. Not only this, Dr. Mishra was also surprised to see an unusual greenery in places in the town. This greenery was not of the 'crop-green' kind but of green cloths with gold-trimmed borders spread over random stones among the ruins.

items.note: Historian Mishra was surprised by signs of obliteration at the temple, palace and other places, including a claimed place of worship of another religion in the temple precinct and a madrasa in the palace; the access to the temple was very narrow due to encroachment (author's characterisation).
items.gloss: However, seeing the marks of erasure of identity at the Paramara-period temple, palace and other places of this obscure town, historian Mishra was astonished. When the evidence of a so-called place of worship of another religion in the temple courtyard, direct proof of a madrasa running in the palace, and the trickery of the green cloths came in the media, the administration woke from sleep. Last year when I came here, the approach road to the huge temple was extremely narrow because of encroachment. From there the temple's grandeur was not even visible.

items.note: The approach path to the temple was extremely narrow due to encroachment, and the temple's grandeur was not visible from it.
items.gloss: Last year when I came here, the approach road to the huge temple was extremely narrow because of encroachment. From there the temple's grandeur was not even visible.

items.note: Historian Mishra's vision that the whole of Udaypur town could be developed as a heritage town; time to remove illegal kiosks.
items.gloss: Historian Dr. Suresh Mishra said that day while returning from Udaypur that the whole of Udaypur town could be developed like a heritage town. Our ancestors could not save the Vijay temple; let us save Udaypur. So now it is time to remove the illegal kiosks.

items.note: Named citizens from Ganj Basoda, Udaypur and Mandi Bamora began; locals first removed encroachments, then built a roughly three-foot-wide cemented road to the temple with public contribution.
items.gloss: And truly some aware citizens became active: the enthusiastic Praveen Sharma, Kaustubh Shirhonkar, Kamlesh Sharma, Gagan Dubey and Amit Shukla of Ganj Basoda; Raja Miyan of Udaypur; Ramiskant Shrivastava of Mandi Bamora and many others. On their initiative first of all the local people themselves began removing the encroachments. After that they took up the task of clearing the blocked path to the temple, and in no time in a small town a cemented road about three feet wide was ready with public cooperation.

items.note: The newly built wide public-funded path makes it seem Udaypur has risen to bring back lost glory.
items.gloss: As if Udaypur had risen to bring back centuries of lost glory. Seeing this newly built wide, broad road built with public cooperation, it seems that such a broad splendid road to the Deccan again and again made outside invaders greedy.

items.note: Describes the route joining Uttarapatha with Dakshinapatha as a highway of devotion along which dynasties built temple towns, and calls the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple one such lamp-post.
items.gloss: That path joining Uttarapatha to Dakshinapatha was not merely a highway of transport but a great path of devotion, on which various dynasties such as Chera, Chola, Pandya, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta built countless temple-towns and cities to keep Indian eternal culture unbroken. From where the stream of devotion lit up the people on all sides. This was the same great path through which the Dravidian-born stream of devotion lit one beacon after another in north India. One such living beacon was the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple of Udaypur.

items.note: Locals who know little of Udaypur's ancient glory are now preparing to become tourism attendants; the history asleep for ten centuries is turning over.
items.gloss: I feel Udaypur is going to get the importance of ancient heritage. Though it will not happen 'right now', certainly the history that slept for ten centuries is gently turning over. Even the residents of this sweet town, who have a little murmur of Udaypur's history but are unaware of its ancient glory, have now begun to gird themselves to become tourism attendants.

items.note: Proposes a tourism circuit for Paramara-period temples across regions to bring domestic religious tourists and curious scholars, and foreign visitors to Khajuraho.
items.gloss: If the state government wishes it can do something new in tourism. If a tourism circuit is created for the conservation of 'Paramara-period temples', joining the north, central, east, west and south regions, domestic tourists will come for religious tourism on a large scale, and the number of occasional curious scholar-type tourists will also increase. Not only this, foreign travellers coming to Khajuraho can also be brought here.

items.note: Says it is time to start the Udaypur chapter of a Paramara tourism circuit, Bhojpur already established, via a PPP model or local cooperation.
items.gloss: The time has now come to begin the Udaypur chapter of the Paramara-period tourism circuit. Bhojpur has already been established. The concept of public private partnership is no longer new. It is known as the PPP model. The government can start this with local cooperation too.

items.note: Important archaeological wealth is scattered across the whole Udaypur town area and within five km; houses within 500 m of the temple are built of ancient material.
items.gloss: Important archaeological wealth lies scattered over the whole Udaypur town area and within a radius of five km around. Houses built just within a five-hundred-metre radius of the temple are built of ancient archaeological material.

items.note: Names such as Udayagiri, Udaypur and Udayasamudra are said to derive from Udayaditya, mentioned as Bhoja's grandson, elsewhere as Bhojabandhu; the Sanchi-area caves were not built by him, he gave the hill his name.
items.gloss: Names such as the famous Udayagiri caves near Vidisha, Udaypur seventy km from Vidisha, and in this same town the Udayasamudra located about five hundred metres in front of the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple are all after Udayaditya, who is mentioned in Paramara history as Bhoja's grandson. In some places he is also mentioned as Bhojabandhu. However, the fifth-century caves near Sanchi were not built by Udayaditya. He gave the hill his name.

claim.value: grandson of Bhoja in Paramara history; elsewhere 'Bhojabandhu' (Vadnerkar)

items.note: Vision statement: Udaypur is now a resolve of awakening, doing something, connecting with one's history.
items.gloss: Udaypur is now a resolve for all of us. A resolve of awakening. A resolve to do something. A resolve to connect with our own history.

items.note: Historian Dr. Mishra's dream: Udaypur as a developed heritage town thronged by history lovers and tourists.
items.gloss: That Udaypur become a developed heritage town, bustling with history lovers and tourists, this alone was his dream, which he has handed over to us. A historian's last dream...
